strings.title: Count Up Through Hundreds and Thousands
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: When the numbers are close to hundreds or thousands, count up from the smaller number: to the next hundred, the next thousand, then the rest.
strings.keywords: count up, distance, hundreds, thousands, friendly numbers
watchFor: Regrouping across zeros and losing track: ask "How far is 2896 from 2900?"
Forgetting a jump when adding them up: ask "Which jumps make the answer?"
Taking a big leap that's hard to add: ask "Could you land on a thousand first?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Which friendly numbers did you land on?" Land: hundreds and thousands make the jumps easy. Count up, then add the jumps: it's the distance between the numbers.

problems.notes: Look for: 100 to 3000, 1000 to 4000. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 2900 >3000 >4000
Look for: 4 to 2900, then 1100, then 3. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Word choice: "the distance from 2896 to 4003". Model: numberline 2896 >2900 >4000 >4003

responses.tip: Regrouping slip. Ask: count up again. Is 2896 + 1207 = 4003?

problems.notes: Look for: 15 to 4000, 2000 to 6000, 12 more. Ask: "What's the first friendly number?" Model: numberline 3985 >4000 >6000 >6012
Look for: 10 to 7900, 100 to 8000, 2000 to 10 000, 5 more. Ask: "How many jumps did you need?" Model: numberline 7890 >7900 >8000 >10000 >10005
Look for: 4 to 19 000, 6000 to 25 000, 4 more. Ask: "Would you count up or slide?" Model: numberline 18996 >19000 >25000 >25004
Look for: 25 to 99 900, 100 to 100 000. Ask: "Are these close together?" Model: numberline 99875 >99900 >100000

responses.tip: Ask: about how far apart are 99 875 and 100 000?

problems.notes: Look for: 5 to 200 000, 100 000 to 300 000, 2 more. Ask: "Does the size of the numbers matter?" Model: numberline 199995 >200000 >300000 >300002

strings.title: Take Too Much, Then Add Back
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: When the number you take away is just under a friendly number, take the friendly number, then add back the extra. With decimals, check which place the extra is in.
strings.keywords: take away a friendly number, add back, compensate, tenths, hundredths, thousandths
watchFor: Adjusting the wrong way (520 − 199 = 520 − 200 − 1): ask "Did you take away too much or too little?"
Adding back the wrong place (12.5 − 4.997 = 12.5 − 5 + 0.03): ask "How far is 4.997 from 5?"
Not seeing that 0.995 is close to 1: ask "What whole number is 0.995 close to?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did you know how much to add back?" Land: find how far the number is from the friendly one (199 is 1 from 200, 4.997 is 0.003 from 5), take the friendly number, then add that back.

problems.notes: Look for: take 200, add 1 back. Ask: "What's 199 close to?" Word choice: "took too much". Model: numberline 520 -200 +1

responses.tip: Ask: did taking 200 take too much or too little?

problems.notes: Look for: take 500, add 2 back. Ask: "How much too much?" Model: numberline 1250 -500 +2
Look for: take 3, add 0.1 back. Ask: "Same move with decimals?" Model: numberline 8.4 -3 +0.1
Look for: take 4, add 0.02 back. Ask: "How far is 3.98 from 4?" Model: numberline 9.15 -4 +0.02

responses.tip: Added back 2 tenths. Ask: is 3.98 two tenths or two hundredths from 4?

problems.notes: Look for: take 5, add 0.003 back. Ask: "Which place is the extra in?" Model: numberline 12.5 -5 +0.003

responses.tip: Ask: how far is 4.997 from 5: 3 hundredths or 3 thousandths?

problems.notes: Look for: take 1, add 0.005 back. Ask: "What's 0.995 close to?" Model: numberline 5 -1 +0.005
Look for: take 20, add 0.2 back. Ask: "Would you use the algorithm here?" Model: numberline 47.3 -20 +0.2
